title.name: Almadía!
title.subtitle: Log rafts down the rivers of Navarra
menu.easy.note: Slower river, softer bumps, no clock.
menu.normal.note: The real river, against the clock.
intro.1: Winter in the Roncal valley. The almadieros cut pines and drag the trunks down to the river.
intro.2: They tie the trunks together with twisted green branches into a long raft: the almadía.
intro.3: Spring arrives. The snow melts and the river rises. Time to take the timber downstream!
outro.1: No almadías carry timber for sale any more, but the tradition is still alive.
outro.2: Every year in Burgui, people still ride almadías down the river. Go see it!
controls.coop: Same way: the raft slides. Opposite ways: it turns.
tip.oars: Each stick swings one end of the raft.
tip.steer: Move the stick to steer the raft.
tip.turn: Push the same way to slide, opposite ways to turn.
tip.straight: The raft is long and heavy: get ready before you reach the rocks.
tip.order: Pass close to the flag to pick up a timber order.
tip.stroke: [A] hard stroke. [B] brace before a bump.
tip.eddy: Logs coming loose? Stop in a calm eddy (the slow swirl) and press [C].
tip.bridge: Bridge! Straighten up and go through an arch.
tip.weir: Weir ahead! Get straight and hit the chute right in the middle.
msg.loose: Ropes loose! One more crash and you'll lose a log. Stop in an eddy and press [C].
msg.lash: Tie up! Press [C] when the ring reaches the raft
msg.lashTogether: Tie up! Both press [C] together when the ring arrives

admin.title: Settings
fact.build: An almadía was built from freshly cut trunks tied with twisted green branches. Long ones were several sections joined in a line.
fact.highways: Before roads and lorries, rivers were the best way to carry Pyrenean timber to faraway towns.
fact.journey: Almadías went down the Esca and Salazar into the Aragón and the Ebro. Some are said to have reached Zaragoza, or even Tortosa.
fact.thaw: Rafts went down in spring, when melting snow raised the rivers high enough to float over the rocks.
fact.oars: Almadieros steered with long oars at the front and back. They had to work together to keep the raft straight.
fact.weirs: Weirs held back water for mills. Shooting through their narrow chute was one of the most dangerous moments of the trip.
fact.walk: After delivering the timber, almadieros usually walked all the way home, a journey that could take many days.
fact.end: The trade faded in the mid-20th century, when lorries, roads and reservoirs took the river's place.
fact.burgui: Every spring, Burgui celebrates the Día de la Almadía, when people ride rafts down the Esca again, as in the old days.
fact.unesco: In 2022, UNESCO recognised timber rafting in Spain and five other European countries as intangible cultural heritage.
course.roncal.name: Stretch 1: Roncal to Burgui
course.roncal.blurb: Down the Esca between the villages of the Roncal valley. A calm stretch to learn on.
course.foz.name: Stretch 2: The Foz de Burgui
course.foz.blurb: The Esca squeezes between rock walls on its way to Sigüés. Watch the rapids!
course.salazar.name: Stretch 3: The Salazar valley
course.salazar.blurb: The neighbouring valley's rafts, from Ochagavía to Lumbier, past fallen trees and the Foz de Arbayún.
course.aragon.name: Stretch 4: The Aragón
course.aragon.blurb: Wide, strong water from Sangüesa to Milagro, with three mill weirs.
course.ebro.name: Stretch 5: The Ebro, to the sea
course.ebro.blurb: The longest run: Tudela, Zaragoza and Tortosa, almost at the Mediterranean.
journey.title: Stretch complete!
tip.gorge: Rock walls! Hitting them loosens the logs. Brake on the bends.
tip.trees: Fallen trees block half the river: go round the other side.
tip.wide: Wide river, strong current. Find each weir's chute early.
tip.ebro: The Ebro! A long way to the sea. Mind the bridges and whirlpools.
fact.foz: The Esca runs through the Foz de Burgui, a rocky gorge where the river is narrow and fast.
fact.salazar: The Salazar valley sent almadías too. They went down the Salazar and the Irati to the Aragón.
